newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria market switches to marks amid lev collapse.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria market switches to marks amid lev collapse.

text.p: Trade switched to German marks at this Bulgarian wholesalers' market on Friday as big falls in the lev raised the spectre of hyperinflation, but the only customers were Serbs and Macedonians.
Handwritten prices were in marks and traders were offering the currency for 250-270 levs. The mark started the week at about 179 levs.
"Trading in marks is normal for me because the lev is constantly tumbling," said a trader selling imported chocolate and coffee at the market on the outskirts of the capital Sofia.
"But we are doing very little business as shopkeepers, who are our main clients, complain they have no customers because of the high prices."
The main buyers were Serbs and Macedonians, buying household items like washing powder, babies' nappies and kitchen equipment in bulk to sell at home.
"We are doing some business only because of the Serbs, without them we would be finished," said one market trader.
Ilientsi is usually geared to trading in marks with Serbian buyers, but the crisis of the past week has reinforced traders' mistrust of the local currency.
Petyo Ivanov, who owns two butcher's shops, said he had closed up because he could no longer make a profit.
"I am here just to check how business is going and I can see that the crisis is in full force," he said.
The lev has fallen about 30 percent against the dollar since Monday as Bulgarians rushed to convert their savings into hard currency.
A clothes seller at Ilientsi who gave her name as Gergana said she was no longer able to earn a living.
"Business has been choked," she said. "My only hope is that Christmas is coming and people may decide to spend some money."

Loss of confidence in the lev and rumours about the likely impact of a currency board, proposed by the International Monetary Fund to stabilise the economy, sparked panic this week. On Thursday alone the lev fell 18 percent.
The dollar is the usual currency of refuge for Bulgarians and many shopkeepers and traders elsewhere in Sofia have started asking for payment in dollars, although this is barred by Bulgarian law.
Bulgarians besieged the State Savings Bank, the country's biggest savings institution, withdrawing more than 14 billion levs since last week.
Some 75 percent of SSB deposits are invested in Treasury paper, and depositors feared the finance ministry might suspend payments on government securities under a currency board.
The IMF says this would not be the case.
A currency board matches the amount of national currency in circulation with the central bank's foreign exchange and gold reserves, effectively pegging the local currency.

Reaction to the proposal has been mixed. While many traders say they would welcome a more predictable exchange rate, the central bank fears a loss of sovereignty, and some businessmen fear it could dry up trade by causing an initial shortage of foreign currency.
